title: Epistaxis (nosebleed) in adults
subject: ophthalmology-ent
setting: Emergency department, ENT outpatients, primary care
summary: Sit the patient up leaning forward and compress the soft lower nose firmly for at least 5 minutes, then clear clots, apply a topical vasoconstrictor, find the bleeding point and cauterise it; pack if the site cannot be seen or bleeding persists (resorbable packs if anticoagulated), and escalate posterior or refractory bleeds to ENT.

sections.title: Triage and history
items: Identify who needs prompt management: ongoing heavy bleeding, haemodynamic instability, airway compromise, or bleeding from both nostrils or down the throat.

Most bleeds are anterior from Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus). Suspect a posterior bleed in older, hypertensive or anticoagulated patients when blood runs into the pharynx despite anterior pressure.
Document bleeding risk factors: anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, personal or family history of bleeding disorders, liver disease, intranasal drug use, recent trauma or nasal surgery.
Recurrent bilateral bleeds with a family history, or telangiectasias of the lips, tongue or fingers, suggest hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT).
Recurrent unilateral bleeding with nasal obstruction needs endoscopy to exclude a tumour (for example nasopharyngeal carcinoma, or juvenile angiofibroma in adolescent males).

sections.title: First aid and resuscitation
items: Sit upright, lean forward, spit out blood rather than swallow it. Do not lie flat or tilt the head back.
Firm continuous compression of the soft lower third of the nose (not the bony bridge) for at least 5 minutes (AAO-HNS); many protocols use 10 to 15 minutes without releasing to check.
Significant bleed: IV access, full blood count, group and save; coagulation screen or INR if anticoagulated or a bleeding disorder is suspected. Resuscitate shock before local measures are complete.

Ask the patient to blow out clots or suction them, then spray or pack the nose with a topical vasoconstrictor and local anaesthetic (oxymetazoline or xylometazoline with lidocaine 4% on pledgets) for about 10 minutes.

sections.title: Anterior bleeding
items: Perform anterior rhinoscopy with a headlight and speculum after removing clot, to find the bleeding point.

Cautery: anaesthetise the site first and apply silver nitrate only to the active or suspected bleeding point, working from the periphery inwards. Avoid cauterising both sides of the septum in the same session (perforation risk).
If the site cannot be seen or bleeding continues, pack the nose: nasal tampon or inflatable balloon pack, or dissolvable (resorbable) material.
Use resorbable packing in patients on anticoagulants or antiplatelets, or with a suspected bleeding disorder.

Topical tranexamic acid (5 mL of 100 mg/mL injection, 500 mg, soaked on pledgets for about 10 minutes) is a reasonable adjunct before packing, including in antiplatelet users; evidence is mixed and a large UK trial (NoPAC) showed no reduction in packing.
Tell the patient the type of pack, when and where it will be removed, aftercare, and warning signs needing return.

sections.title: Posterior or refractory bleeding
items: Bleeding despite a correctly placed anterior pack, or blood seen trickling down the oropharynx: refer urgently to ENT.

Posterior packing (posterior balloon catheter, or a Foley catheter with an anterior pack) needs admission with continuous SpO2 monitoring, analgesia and watch for hypoxaemia, especially in the elderly and those with lung disease.
Nasal endoscopy to locate the bleeding site for recurrent bleeding despite packing or cautery, or recurrent unilateral bleeding.
Persistent or recurrent bleeding not controlled by packing or cautery: consider endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or endovascular embolisation.

sections.title: Anticoagulants, HHT and children
items: Unless bleeding is life-threatening, start first-line measures (compression, vasoconstrictor, cautery, resorbable packing) before transfusion, reversal or withdrawal of anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs.

Check INR on warfarin; manage a raised INR or life-threatening bleeding with the anticoagulant reversal protocol. Do not stop anticoagulants or antiplatelets without weighing the thrombotic risk with the prescriber.
HHT: refer to a specialist; prefer resorbable packs and gentle measures, as repeated cautery damages the mucosa.
Children 3 years and older usually have minor anterior bleeds from dry mucosa or nose picking. Epistaxis under 2 years is unusual: consider injury, non-accidental injury or a bleeding disorder.

sections.title: Discharge and prevention
items: Discharge after an anterior bleed is controlled and the patient is stable; posterior packs, recurrent bleeding, anaemia or major comorbidity usually need admission.
Advise nasal lubrication (petroleum jelly or saline gel), humidification, avoiding nose picking, forceful blowing and straining for a few days, and how to do first aid at home.
Give clear return advice: bleeding not stopping with 15 minutes of pressure, heavy bleeding, dizziness or fainting.
Arrange documented follow-up within 30 days for patients treated with non-resorbable packing, surgery or embolisation. Treat hypertension per usual standards once the bleed is controlled.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Pressing on the bony bridge, or releasing pressure every minute to check.
Lying the patient flat or tilting the head back, causing swallowed blood, vomiting and aspiration.
Bilateral septal cautery in one sitting.
Missing a posterior bleed, a tumour in recurrent unilateral epistaxis, or hypoxaemia after posterior packing.
Reflexly stopping or reversing anticoagulants for a bleed controlled by local measures.

drugs.name: Oxymetazoline 0.05% nasal spray
drugs.dose: 2 sprays into the bleeding nostril, or on cotton pledgets for about 10 minutes
drugs.notes: Xylometazoline 0.1% is the common alternative in India.

drugs.name: Lidocaine (lignocaine) 4% topical
drugs.dose: On cotton pledgets with the vasoconstrictor for about 10 minutes before cautery
drugs.notes: Keep total lidocaine within the maximum safe dose (4.5 mg/kg).

drugs.name: Silver nitrate cautery stick
drugs.dose: Apply to the identified bleeding point only for a few seconds after topical anaesthesia
drugs.notes: One side of the septum per session.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid (topical)
drugs.dose: 500 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/mL injection) soaked on pledgets, left in the bleeding nostril for about 10 minutes
